headline: Open, dawn and empty are three spellings of one sound: あける.
A word with a known inventor and year, and little else on record.
A futon began as a Zen meditation cushion made of bulrush, not cloth.
“Skin and flesh” became “sarcasm” through a Zen test of understanding.
One spelling, two unrelated words: a Chinese compound and a lost native one.
“Plum rain” on paper, つゆ in speech, and no certain origin for the sound.
From “adding it all up” to “is that convenient for you?”
Autumn may be kin to “bright”, “red” and “full up” — though Wiktionary says the exact relationship remains unclear.
Fog is a verb turned noun: kiri is the stem of kiru, “to become foggy”.
Dew is tsuyu, and Wiktionary can trace it no further back than Old Japanese.
Frost may be the “low” word: shimo is thought to be cognate with, or derived from, 下 (“bottom, lower part”).
Tree is ki, with a Ryukyuan cousin *ke, and it is first attested in the Kojiki of 712 CE.
Leaf, feather, tooth, blade: Wiktionary lists them as possible kin, then notes that their pitch accents disagree.
A forest as a heap: mori is probably cognate with 盛り (“heap, pile”), from how woods look from a distance.
A hayashi may have been a deliberately planted grove: the word derives from the transitive verb 生やす (“to grow”).
Mountain and forest in one: Proto-Japonic *yama meant “mountain; forest”.
Rivers once had a p: Old Japanese kapa is the ancestor of kawa.
A bridge is “the space between”: hashi is cognate with words for stairs, narrow gaps and squeezing.
A barber’s is a “raised-floor shop”: barbershops were historically often 床店, stalls on a raised floor.
Machi first meant a “plot of land”, and Vovin argues it was borrowed from a Korean ancestor word for “field”.
A village is either “a gathering” (from 群れる) or a word from Old Korean — the source does not pick.
A station began as a relay post where horses were changed.
Literally an “electric vehicle”: 電 (den) + 車 (sha).
Before it meant “umbrella”, 傘 was a rain hat made of bundled reeds or sedges.
Rain and candy are both ame today, but Wiktionary keeps them as distinct Old Japanese words, ame2 and ame1.
The candy ame is its own word, kept apart from 雨 (“rain”) as ⟨ame1⟩.
Reconstructed as Proto-Japonic *kansai — with an n that modern kaze no longer has.
Cloud is kumo: attested in the Kojiki of 712 CE and reconstructed back to Proto-Japonic *kumo.
Thunder was originally “god” + “cry out”: 神 (kami) + 鳴り (nari).
The rainbow may once have been nuji or noji: the source suggests a shift from those earlier readings.
Many theories for “rice”, from “doing with one's heart” to Austronesian cousins — the last called extremely speculative.
